title: Against slavery
hook: slow at first, Emerson came to speak strongly against slavery

segments.voice: Yesterday, Margaret Fuller, who asked that every path be opened to women. Your line was equal minds. Did you get to hear the end of someone's thought? Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

An honest thing to say about a man this path has spent weeks with: on the great moral wound of his country, Emerson was slow. He believed slavery was wrong. He said so in his journals. But for a long stretch he kept mostly to his study and his lectures, wary of crowds and causes and movements. Others around him moved sooner. By the usual account, his own wife was involved in antislavery work in Concord before he was. And people who had escaped slavery themselves were already speaking out, at a risk he never faced. Then something changed, and the quiet man in the study stood up. Today is about what moved him, and what it cost to stop being careful.
screen: `HE BELIEVED IT WAS WRONG.` → `HE STAYED IN THE STUDY.` → `THEN HE STOOD UP.`

segments.voice: First, the reasons he gave himself for waiting. Emerson distrusted joining things. Self-reliance, for him, meant reforming your own soul before reforming the world, and he worried that causes could swallow a person whole. There's something real in that worry. There's also something convenient in it, and later readers have said so plainly. Second, what changed. His country passed the Fugitive Slave Law, which required people in free states to help return those who had escaped slavery. Now it was no longer a wrong happening somewhere else. It reached into Concord and asked him to cooperate. In his journal he wrote, in effect, that he would not obey it. Third, what he did. He began speaking in public, and sharply. He turned against Daniel Webster, a statesman he had long admired, for supporting the law. He spoke for the cause, and he welcomed the abolitionist John Brown to Concord. Whatever one thinks of every choice he made, the careful man had stopped being careful. Fourth, the lesson for an ordinary day. Emerson's case shows how a good person can hold the right belief for years and still keep it indoors. Agreeing silently felt like enough, until something made it impossible. Speaking up isn't the same as being loud about everything. It's the moment when a private conviction walks out of the study, into a room where it might cost you something.
screen: `REFORM THE SOUL FIRST.` · `THE LAW REACHED INTO CONCORD.` · `HE TURNED ON A MAN HE ADMIRED.` · `THE CONVICTION LEAVES THE STUDY.` · then, large: `SPEAK UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you believe that has stayed indoors. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind go to something you think is wrong, near you, not far away. At work, at school, in the family. Not the biggest thing in the world. The nearest. Notice the reasons you've given for staying quiet. Some of them might be wise. Some might just be comfortable. Don't sort them yet. Just picture one sentence you could say about it, plainly, to one person. Hold that sentence. The bell holds the time.
Against slavery. Emerson believed slavery was wrong for years before he spoke strongly; a law that asked for his cooperation brought him out of his study. Today's word.
Your line: speak up. Today, say the one sentence you found, once, to the person who needs to hear it. Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Readers of Emerson often study his later antislavery speeches alongside his early caution, as a case of a private conviction becoming public action.

fork.setup: you're Emerson. you've believed slavery is wrong for years, but you distrust causes. now a law asks your town to help return people who escaped. what do you do?
options: keep reforming your own soul quietly.
speak publicly against the law, even against a man you admired.
move somewhere the law doesn't reach.
fork.reveal: he began speaking sharply in public, and turned against Daniel Webster for supporting the law.

trapdoor: what you thought: Emerson was an abolitionist from the start.
what it means: he believed slavery was wrong but was slow to act; the Fugitive Slave Law brought him out to speak strongly.
what a scholar hears: his early caution came partly from his own philosophy, reform the self before joining causes, which later readers have both understood and criticized.

notes: Editor pass: replaced the uncited ranking 'spoke first and risked the most' about people who had escaped slavery with a plain statement that they were already speaking at greater risk.
No dates are given under the claims rule (the 1844 West Indies emancipation address, the 1850 law, the 1851 Concord address are all omitted). Confirm the sequence as told.
Journal paraphrase: Emerson's 1851 journal is commonly quoted as 'I will not obey it, by God.' The script paraphrases. Confirm.
'By the usual account, his own wife was involved in antislavery work in Concord before he was': Lidian Emerson and the Concord Female Anti-Slavery Society. Confirm wording.

John Brown's visits to Concord and Emerson's support are mentioned briefly, with 'whatever one thinks of every choice he made'. A reviewer should check this is handled carefully, given Brown's violence.
The line about people who escaped slavery speaking first and risking most is general history; a reviewer may want a named example (e.g., Frederick Douglass) or to soften.
